title: NLP, transformers and language models
summary: From text to tokens to a working GPT you understand line by line: tokenization (with Urdu cost realities), neural LMs, self-attention, the Transformer block and modern variants, pretraining, decoding and KV-cache inference, then HF library fluency. Spine: Karpathy Zero to Hero + Raschka LLMs-from-scratch; HF LLM Course for library fluency. U01–U04 only need M03 Python and can run before M10.

units.title: The LLM lifecycle in one sitting
outcomes: You can draw the pipeline pretraining data → base model → SFT → RL → deployed assistant and say what each stage changes.
You can predict how a base model and its instruct sibling respond differently to the same prompt.
You can explain hallucination as fluent output unsupported by training data or context, and name mitigations (tools, retrieval, refusal training).

practice.title: Base vs instruct, side by side
practice.brief: Pick one model family with a base and an instruct checkpoint on the HF Hub (e.g. Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct). Send both the same 5 prompts (a question, an instruction, a half-written email, a list, a harmful request) with the instruct model's chat template applied only to the instruct model. Log the outputs, then draw a one-page lifecycle diagram labelling which stage explains each difference.
practice.done_when: A notebook or script with 10 logged generations (5 prompts × 2 models), plus a diagram image/markdown that labels each observed difference with the training stage responsible.

quiz.prompt: A base (pretrained-only) model given 'What is the capital of France?' most likely:
options: Continues the text, possibly by writing more quiz questions
quiz.explain: A base model has only learned to continue documents; assistant behaviour comes from post-training.

quiz.prompt: Hallucination is best described as:
options: A sampling bug in the decoder
Fluent output not supported by training data or the provided context
quiz.explain: The model produces plausible continuations whether or not it has the knowledge; Karpathy frames this as the statistical simulation of a confident labeller.

quiz.prompt: Which stage changes assistant-like behaviour most while using the least data?
quiz.explain: Post-training uses orders of magnitude less data than pretraining but shapes format, tone and helpfulness.

quiz.prompt: Why does 'the model knows X' not imply 'the model will say X correctly when asked'?
rubric: Distinguishes knowledge stored in weights (lossy, probabilistic) from what sampling produces for a given prompt
Mentions at least one cause: sampling randomness, prompt phrasing, tokenization, or post-training not teaching the model to surface/abstain
Gives a mitigation such as retrieval, tool use, or training the model to say 'I don't know'

practice.title: Bilingual bigram LM with normalization
practice.brief: Collect ~1 MB English and ~1 MB Urdu (Nastaliq or Roman) public-domain text. Normalize with unicodedata.normalize (NFC and NFKC) and find one string where normalization changes the character/token count. Train a bigram LM with add-one smoothing per language and report held-out perplexity. Train a small word2vec (gensim) on the English half and list the 5 nearest neighbours for 5 words.
practice.done_when: Script prints held-out perplexity for both languages, shows one before/after normalization example with differing lengths, and lists word2vec neighbours; README explains one failure on code-mixed text.

quiz.prompt: NFKC normalization can:
options: Map compatibility characters (e.g. ligatures, full-width forms) to a canonical form
quiz.explain: NFKC applies compatibility decomposition then canonical composition; it changes visually similar code points, not language.

quiz.prompt: Add-one (Laplace) smoothing in n-gram LMs exists to:
options: Avoid zero probability for n-grams unseen in training
quiz.explain: A single unseen bigram would otherwise give the whole test sentence probability zero (infinite perplexity).

quiz.prompt: word2vec's skip-gram objective predicts:
options: Context words from a centre word
quiz.explain: Skip-gram learns embeddings by predicting surrounding words; CBOW does the reverse.

quiz.prompt: Give one concrete reason a word-level vocabulary fails on Urdu/English code-mixed chat.
rubric: Names a specific mechanism: spelling variation in Roman Urdu (e.g. 'nahi'/'nahin'), script mixing, or out-of-vocabulary rates
Connects it to unknown tokens or exploding vocabulary size
Points to subword/byte-level tokenization as the remedy

practice.title: minbpe-style tokenizer + language cost report
practice.brief: Implement byte-level BPE (train/encode/decode) yourself, with a round-trip test over 1,000 random Unicode strings (include Urdu and emoji). Train it on mixed English/Urdu text at vocab 1k and 4k. For the same paragraph in English, Urdu (Nastaliq) and Roman Urdu, report tokens per word with your tokenizer and with tiktoken o200k_base, and write the API-cost implication at a stated price per 1M tokens.
practice.done_when: All round-trip tests pass (decode(encode(s)) == s); a table shows tokens/word for 3 language variants × 3 tokenizers; README states the cost ratio Urdu:English.

quiz.prompt: Byte-level BPE guarantees:
options: No unknown tokens, because every byte is in the base vocabulary
quiz.explain: Any string is a byte sequence and all 256 bytes are base tokens, so encoding never fails.

quiz.prompt: A frequent cause of LLMs failing at counting letters in a word is:
options: Tokens spanning multiple characters, so the model never sees individual letters
quiz.explain: Karpathy shows 'strawberry'-style failures trace back to multi-character tokens.

quiz.prompt: Each step of BPE training:
options: Merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token
quiz.explain: BPE is a greedy compression algorithm over pair frequencies.

quiz.prompt: Why can the same API request cost noticeably more in Urdu than in English?
rubric: Explains that tokenizers trained on English-heavy data have fewer merges for Urdu, so more tokens per word
Links tokens to billing and to context/latency (more tokens = more cost and slower)
Gives a measured or estimated ratio, or names a mitigation (model with better multilingual tokenizer, shorter prompts)

practice.brief: Batch three sentences of different lengths through a small model (distilbert for classification, and a small causal LM). Show logits differ when you drop attention_mask. quiz.prompt: In the attention mask, padding positions are set so that:
options: Padding tokens receive zero attention weight
quiz.explain: Mask value 0 → the score is set to −∞ before softmax, so padding contributes nothing.

quiz.prompt: Truncation that silently drops the end of a document mostly risks:
quiz.explain: Truncation is silent by default; the lost text is simply not seen by the model.

quiz.prompt: Decoder-only batched generation usually pads on the:
quiz.explain: New tokens are appended on the right, so real tokens must be contiguous at the right edge.

quiz.prompt: What bug appears in a RAG system if chunks are truncated by the embedding model's max length without logging?
rubric: Identifies that the tail of long chunks is never embedded, so queries matching that text fail to retrieve it
Notes it is silent: no error, just lower recall
Proposes a fix: chunk below max length, or log/alert on truncation

quiz.prompt: A perplexity of 1 on a test set means:
options: The model predicts every test token with probability 1
quiz.explain: PPL = exp(mean NLL); NLL = 0 only when every correct token gets probability 1.

quiz.prompt: The main practical weakness of vanilla RNNs that Transformers address is:
options: Sequential computation plus vanishing gradients over long ranges
quiz.explain: RNNs process tokens one at a time (no parallelism over time) and struggle to carry gradients far back.

quiz.prompt: Cross-entropy loss for next-token prediction is:
options: The negative log-probability the model assigns to the correct next token
Mean squared error of the logits
KL divergence to the uniform distribution
quiz.explain: Karpathy derives it directly from the likelihood of the training data.

quiz.prompt: Why can't you compare perplexities of two models with different tokenizers directly?
rubric: States that perplexity is per token, and the token unit differs between tokenizers
Gives the fix: normalize to bits-per-byte/character or per word
Optional: mentions sliding-window/context-length effects

practice.brief: Implement single-head then multi-head causal self-attention in PyTorch. quiz.prompt: Scaling attention scores by √d_k prevents:
options: Softmax saturation caused by large dot products
quiz.explain: Dot products grow with dimension; large logits push softmax to one-hot and kill gradients.

quiz.prompt: In causal self-attention, the mask sets future positions to:
quiz.explain: −∞ becomes weight 0 after softmax; setting 0 before softmax would still give them weight.

quiz.prompt: Multi-head attention mainly lets the model:
options: Attend to different relation types in different representation subspaces
quiz.explain: Each head has its own projections, so heads can specialise.

quiz.prompt: How does attention cost grow with sequence length n, and why does that matter for long-context apps?
rubric: States O(n²) time/memory for the score matrix (per layer, per head)
Connects it to latency/cost of long prompts or long documents
Mentions a mitigation (FlashAttention, sparse/sliding attention, retrieval instead of stuffing)

quiz.prompt: Residual connections primarily:
options: Ease gradient flow through deep stacks

quiz.prompt: RoPE encodes position by:

quiz.prompt: For sentence embeddings used in retrieval, the most common architecture family is:

quiz.prompt: The KV cache avoids:
options: Recomputing keys and values for past tokens at every decode step
quiz.explain: Past K/V are reused; only the new token's K/V are computed each step.

quiz.prompt: Time-to-first-token is dominated by:
quiz.explain: The whole prompt must be processed before the first output token exists.

quiz.prompt: KV-cache memory grows linearly with:
quiz.explain: Each token in each sequence stores K and V per layer.
